title: Applying DFT to Organic Chemistry – Part B

quiz.q: In the Diels–Alder reaction (4a) two π bonds become two new σ bonds. Why is error cancellation likely to be *worse* here than for the ethane rotation of Experiment 3?
options: The bonding changes a lot between reactants and product, so errors in describing each bond type no longer cancel
The molecules are larger, so the basis set is incomplete
The reference value is less accurate
quiz.explain: Error cancellation works best when reactants and products are chemically similar. Turning π bonds into σ bonds changes the electron density substantially, so each functional's systematic errors don't cancel.

quiz.q: What holds the ethane dimer (4c) together?
quiz.explain: Ethane has no dipole and no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The ~1.3 kcal/mol of binding is almost entirely dispersion: correlated fluctuations of the electron clouds.

quiz.q: Many older functionals (e.g. B3LYP, PBE) miss most of the dispersion energy. For a dispersion-bound dimer they typically predict binding that is…
quiz.explain: Semilocal and hybrid functionals depend on the density at (or near) each point, so they cannot describe the long-range correlation behind dispersion. Corrections such as D4 or nonlocal VV10 add it back.

quiz.q: Branched alkanes are slightly more stable than their linear isomers. What sign do you expect for ΔE of *n*-hexane → neohexane (4b)?
quiz.explain: The product (neohexane) is lower in energy, so ΔE = Σ νᵢEᵢ < 0. Getting this small difference right is surprisingly hard for many functionals: it is partly a medium-range dispersion effect.
